feedback: If a learner predicts 'fewer than 4 because dividing shrinks', treat it as the teachable moment: lay the tiles and count to 20 together, then name the principle — a small divisor means many copies fit.
If a learner reads 4 ÷ 1/5 as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8, rebuild what 1/5 IS (one part of a whole split five ways) and re-ask 'how many of THOSE fit in 4?'
If a learner computes 4 × 1/5 = 4/5, separate the two questions explicitly: '4 × 1/5 means four fifths; 4 ÷ 1/5 means how many fifths in four', and model both on the same bar.
activities.intendedInsight: When the piece is small, many copies fit, so dividing a positive whole number by a fraction between 0 and 1 produces a count larger than the dividend. The quotient is something you can physically count, not a trick.
learnerActions: Take a 4-unit strip/bar and a stack of 1/5 tiles (ribbon lengths or number-line jumps work equally well).
BEFORE placing any tile, write down a prediction of how many 1/5 tiles will fit, and a one-sentence reason.
Lay the 1/5 tiles end-to-end across the bar, counting as you go: 5 fill the first whole, 10 the second, and so on until you reach 20.
Compare the count (20) with your prediction, and discuss why the answer is bigger than 4.
Repeat with a different piece size (e.g. 1/2 gives 8, 1/10 gives 40) and describe how the size of the piece drives the count.
activities.title: How many fit? Predict then count on a length bar

feedback: If a learner cannot say whether the answer grows or shrinks, return to the 'how many fit' question with a concrete piece.
Praise reasoning that ties the estimate to the piece size relative to 1 whole (e.g. 'the piece is nearly a whole, so a bit more than 5').
activities.intendedInsight: Estimation acts as a reasonableness check: an answer of 0.8 for 4 ÷ 1/5 is immediately caught as absurd because many small fifths must fit in 4 wholes.
learnerActions: Before computing, estimate whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the dividend, and roughly how big.
Work an example like 5 ÷ 5/6: reason that because 5/6 is nearly 1 whole, the answer is a little more than 5.
Check a worked answer for reasonableness: decide whether 0.8 could possibly be the answer to 4 ÷ 1/5, and explain why not.
State a rule of thumb: dividing by a piece smaller than 1 gives more copies than the number of wholes.
activities.title: Estimate first to catch absurd answers

feedback: If a learner cannot form the inverse, prompt: 'If 20 fifths make up 4, what multiplication says that?'
If the inverse product does not rebuild the dividend, revisit the count rather than accepting the quotient.
activities.intendedInsight: Division by a unit fraction and the related multiplication are inverse statements about the same quantity, so the multiplication check confirms the division.
learnerActions: After counting 20 fifths in 4 wholes, write the matching multiplication: 20 × 1/5 = 4.
Explain in words how the multiplication just learned justifies the division answer.
Gather or redraw the 20 fifths into 4 wholes to show the multiplication rebuilding the original dividend.
Apply the same check to a fresh case, e.g. verify 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24 by showing 24 × 1/4 = 6.
activities.title: Prove it with the inverse multiplication

feedback: If a learner's story does not match a 'how many small pieces fit in a whole amount' structure, help reshape it before solving.
Draw out the prediction step: a learner who expects fewer scoops has surfaced the shrink misconception, which the count then resolves.
activities.intendedInsight: Owning the measurement structure through a self-made context makes the 'how many fit' meaning transferable rather than memorised.
learnerActions: Invent a real context for a whole ÷ unit-fraction, e.g. 'how many 1/4-cup scoops are in 6 cups?' or 'how many 1/3-cup scoops in this jug?'
Before counting, predict out loud whether there will be more or fewer scoops than the number of whole cups, and say why.
Solve the story by counting the pieces and state the answer with its meaning.
Match several division expressions (e.g. 6 ÷ 1/4, 4 ÷ 1/5) to the correct 'how many … in …' story.
activities.title: Invent and solve a measurement story
